text.p: Electrical engineering group ABB Asea Brown Boveri AG reported a lower 1996 group net profit on Thursday and said it expected 1997 net income to reach at least the same level as in 1996.

ABB reported 1996 group net income of $1.233 billion compared with $1.315 billion in 1995, which was inflated by a one-off gain of $250 million for putting its transport business in a joint venture with Germany's Daimler-Benz AG.
The group also raised dividends on the shares of its two holding companies, Swiss ABB AG and Swedish ABB AB, who each control half the group.

"If we can keep at least the same (profit) level for 1997 as in 1996, then we come out of the recession, the downturn in the economy, much better than compared with the last," newly appointed president and chief executive Goran Lindahl said.
ABB said group profits improved at all levels and net profit, excluding the one-off gain, rose 15.8 percent to $1.233 billion from an adjusted $1.065 billion.
Lindahl said ABB had clearly warned markets about the slowdown in 1996 and 1997 and its 1996 results should be compared with the adjusted 1995 results.
"The operations are definitely better in 1996 than in 1995," Lindahl said.
The stock market reacted with disappointment and shares of Swiss parent ABB AG fell 5.3 percent to close at 1,714 Swiss francs. Shares in Sweden's ABB AB fell 5.4 percent to 850 crowns.
Industry analysts said they remained confident about ABB's earnings prospects.
Emerging from a briefing by ABB executives, analysts said the stock market's negative reaction was excessive but understandable in light of high expectations.
"The market had forgotten how intense competition is," said Frederick Hasslauer of Bank Sal. Oppenheim, adding that other companies could also dash expectations.
"The market has become overheated," said Peter Gachnang of Bank Julius Baer.
But instead of blaming ABB for their expectations, analysts said they had been too optimistic and ABB had often warned that 1996 and 1997 would be tough years.
ABB said operating earnings totalled $3.026 billion as compared to $3.275 billion for 1995.
The group also proposed a 10-for-one split of Swedish holding company ABB AB's A and B shares, a move that would lower the par value of shares to 5.0 Swedish crowns from 50 crowns.
The group is proposing a reduction of the par value of Swiss parent ABB AG's bearer shares to 50 Swiss francs from 100 francs and the par value of the registered shares to 10 francs from 20.
The dividends on the ABB AG's bearer and registered shares were raised to 38 francs and 7.60 francs, respectively, from 1995 levels of 30 francs and six francs.
The dividend on ABB AB's stock was raised to 17.50 crowns from 16.00 crowns.
Commenting on the outlook for 1997, ABB said it expected the global market for new power plants to expand in emerging markets but remain at a low level in industrial nations.
"Within this competitive environment, 1997 orders and earnings for the power generation segment are expected to reach at least the 1996 level," ABB said in a statement.
